analysis.one_liner: Extends all Bush-era income tax rates for two years, cuts payroll taxes, and renews unemployment benefits.
analysis.headline: The December 2010 tax deal became law on December 17, after the House had first passed a version limiting rate extensions to households under $250,000 and the Senate then pushed through the full two-year package, 81-19 in the Senate and 277-148 in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 4853 began in March 2010 as a routine extension of FAA and highway funding [S2]. After the Senate amended it in September [S4], Congress in December used the still-open bill as the vehicle for the negotiated year-end tax package: all of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts were extended through 2012 for every income level, the estate tax returned at a 35% maximum rate with a $5 million exclusion, unemployment benefits were extended into mid-2012, and employees got a two-percentage-point payroll tax cut for 2011 [S6]. The House first passed a version making the cuts permanent only for households under $200,000 ($250,000 married) [S5], but the Senate loaded the bill with the full two-year deal for all incomes and won final approval in both chambers [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: If it passes: middle-class families keep lower income-tax rates and the expanded child, earned income, and education credits through 2012 [S6]; long-term unemployed workers keep federal emergency benefits through early June 2012 [S6]; every employee gets a payroll tax cut of two percentage points in 2011, with Social Security made whole by a Treasury transfer [S6]; high-income households keep the 15% capital gains and dividend rates for two more years [S6]; large estates get a 35% maximum tax with a $5 million per-person exclusion, plus the ability of a surviving spouse to inherit the unused exclusion [S6]; and businesses get 100% expensing of equipment placed in service through 2011, a longer list of tax extenders (research credit, biofuel credits, film expensing, oil and gas depletion relief), and relief from the alternative minimum tax through 2011 [S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Middle-class workers, the long-term unemployed, businesses, high earners

how_it_helps.text: Extends through December 31, 2012 the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts — individual income tax rates, the 15% rate on capital gains and dividends, and the expanded child tax credit, earned income tax credit, and education credits — for taxpayers at every income level [S6].
Extends federal Emergency Unemployment Compensation, with the last date to enter the program moved to January 3, 2012 and the program running until June 9, 2012, on top of state benefits [S6].
Cuts the employee payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 4.2% for calendar year 2011, with Treasury transfers replacing the Social Security trust funds' lost revenue [S6].

Allows 100% expensing of qualified business equipment placed in service after September 8, 2010 and before 2012, and extends dozens of expiring tax provisions including the research credit, biodiesel and ethanol credits, and film production expensing [S6].
Provides alternative minimum tax relief through 2011, protecting middle-income taxpayers who would otherwise be caught by the AMT's rising reach [S6].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, because the extensions carry no revenue offsets — the Act designates itself an emergency requirement, which exempts its budget cost from pay-as-you-go discipline, so the cost is added to the deficit and borne by future taxpayers through borrowing [S6]. Within the tax code, the estate-tax change is a direct revenue loss concentrated on the largest inheritances, and the extended energy and business credits are paid for by all taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury, deficit, and future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The estate tax returns at a maximum 35% rate with a $5 million exclusion per person (and spousal portability), sharply cheaper than the 55% rate and $1 million exclusion that was scheduled to return in 2011 — a benefit concentrated on very large estates [S6].

Nothing in the Act pays for its cost: it designates itself an emergency requirement under the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act, which is the mechanism for adding the entire package to the deficit rather than offsetting it [S6].

The extenders include targeted industry provisions — suspension of the taxable-income limit on percentage depletion for oil and gas from marginal wells, an ethanol import tariff extension, and film and motorsports tax breaks — each of which directs federal money to a specific industry [S6].
Everything is a two-year patch that expires after 2012, which locked in a cycle of repeated end-of-year standoffs over the same tax questions [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The help for ordinary people was real and immediate: unemployment benefits kept flowing during a 9%-plus-unemployment economy, the payroll tax cut reached nearly every worker, and middle-class families avoided a broad tax increase scheduled for January 2011. But the price was high and unevenly distributed. The same vote extended the top rates and rewrote the estate tax at 35% with a $5 million exclusion — the single most concentrated giveaway in the package — and none of it was offset, so the whole deal was financed by borrowing. A House majority had first approved a version that made the cuts permanent only for households under $250,000; the final law gave the two years to everyone, which is where the largest additional cost to the Treasury lies.

outcome.mechanism: Congress folded the negotiated two-year tax deal into this small aviation-funding bill: after the House passed a narrower version 234-188, the Senate cut off amendment attempts with an 83-15 cloture vote and passed the full package 81-19, the House agreed 277-148, and the President signed it on December 17, 2010.

narrative.text: Introduced March 16, 2010 as a Federal Aviation Administration and surface transportation funding extension, the bill passed the House the next day by voice vote under a suspension-of-the-rules shortcut reserved for noncontroversial bills [S9].
On September 23, 2010, the Senate passed the bill with an amendment by unanimous consent, replacing it with a further airport-funding extension [S4].

On December 2, 2010, the House used the bill as the vehicle for a tax package making the 2001/2003 tax benefits permanent for taxpayers under $200,000 ($250,000 married), agreeing to the Senate amendment with an amendment, 234-188, with Democrats in favor 231-20 and Republicans opposed 3-168 [S5].

The Senate majority then substituted the full negotiated deal: a December 9 motion to send the House message back to the Finance Committee with instructions to make further changes fell 65-11, cloture on the Senate's own version (SA 4753) was invoked 83-15, and three attempts to suspend the rules to offer amendments — by Coburn (47-52), DeMint (37-63), and Sanders (43-57) — were all defeated [S9].
The Senate concurred in the House amendment with the Senate's amendment 81-19 on December 15, with 13 of 56 Democrats, 5 of 42 Republicans, and the lone independent voting no [S16].

The House agreed to the final Senate version 277-148 on the last vote, with Democrats split 139-112 and Republicans in favor 138-36, and the President signed it the next day as Public Law 111-312 [S17].

The enacted law extends all of the Bush-era tax cuts through 2012 for every income level — not just the under-$250,000 households the House version had covered — and adds the estate-tax rewrite, unemployment extension, and payroll tax cut [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households, large estates, and capital-intensive businesses came out ahead on the money: they kept the top-rate cuts and capital-gains rates for two more years and got an estate tax at 35% with a $5 million exclusion after the House's narrower version had limited rate extensions to households under $250,000. Long-term unemployed workers also genuinely gained, with benefits extended into mid-2012, but the largest new concessions beyond current policy went to the top.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, large estates — and jobless benefits recipients

sides.party_line_note: The deal was bipartisan but split both parties: the final Senate vote was 81-19 with 13 of 56 Democrats and 5 of 42 Republicans opposed, and the final House vote was 277-148 with Democrats divided 139-112 while Republicans backed it 138-36; the House's earlier December 2 version had been nearly all-Democratic (231-20) against near-unanimous Republican opposition (3-168).

industries.note: The law extends the top income-tax rates and 15% capital gains/dividend rates for two years and reinstates the estate tax at a 35% maximum with a $5 million per-person exclusion and spousal portability — terms far cheaper than the pre-2001 schedule that was scheduled to return. These benefits concentrate on the wealthiest households and are paid for by all taxpayers through deficit borrowing [S6].

Businesses get 100% expensing of equipment placed in service through 2011, extended bonus depreciation, AMT relief, and the research credit, which lowers the cost of investment. The revenue cost is carried by all taxpayers since nothing is offset [S6].

The law extends the suspension of the taxable-income limitation on percentage depletion for oil and gas from marginal wells through 2011, a targeted tax benefit to the industry paid for by the Treasury [S6].

Credits for biodiesel, renewable diesel, ethanol, and alternative fuel mixtures are extended through 2011, along with the tariff on imported ethanol. The credits support domestic production but the ethanol tariff raises fuel input costs for blenders and consumers [S6].

The original vehicle — extended aviation fuel and ticket excise taxes, Airport and Airway Trust Fund expenditure authority, and airport improvement grants — remains part of the enacted law, keeping airport construction funding and FAA operations financed through the trust fund [S2, S7].
